title: Leave no passphrase behind after unlocking the vault

blocks.text: Operators unlock the deployment vault by typing a passphrase at a console, which hands it over as a `char[]`, sometimes with a trailing `'\n'`. After an incident, the security team took a heap dump of the deploy tool and found the passphrase in it twice, long after the unlock had finished.

The vault's client library takes the passphrase without the newline, reads it during `open`, and keeps no reference to it. Write `unlock(typed)` in `src/main/java/practice/VaultUnlock.java`: it opens the vault and returns the session id, or lets the vault's `IllegalArgumentException` for a wrong passphrase reach the caller. `passphraseLength(typed)` is there to help.
When `unlock` has returned or thrown, every `char[]` that held the passphrase, the operator's included, holds only `'\0'`. About seven lines in total.

cases.says: the vault receives the passphrase without the console's trailing newline, and unlock returns its session id
a passphrase typed without a trailing newline is passed on whole
the vault's refusal of a wrong passphrase reaches the caller
the operator's array is wiped even when the vault refuses the passphrase
the array the vault was handed, a copy made without the newline, is wiped after the call
the operator's own array is wiped after a successful unlock, not only the copy

origin.section: Wiping a char[] Removes Your Copy of a Secret; a String Copy Stays Until GC

concepts: A secret held in char[] is wiped in a finally block, in the caller's array and in every copy the code made.
